'''''Setaria''''' is a widespread genus of plants in the [[Poaceae|grass family]].<ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/394130#page/135/mode/1up Palisot de Beauvois, Ambroise Marie François Joseph. 1812.  Essai d'une Nouvelle Agrostographie  page 51] in Latin</ref><ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/394130#page/298/mode/1up Palisot de Beauvois, Ambroise Marie François Joseph. 1812.  Essai d'une Nouvelle Agrostographie plate XIII (13), figure III (3)] line drawing of ''Setaria viridis''</ref> The name is derived from the [[Latin]] word ''seta'', meaning "bristle" or "hair", which refers to the bristly spikelets.<ref name="CRC">{{cite book |last = Quattrocchi |first=Umberto |title=CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology |volume=4: R-Q |year=2000 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=0-8493-2673-7 |page=2470}}</ref>

The genus includes over 100 species distributed in many tropical and temperate regions around the world,<ref name=ali>Aliscioni, S., et al. [http://2004.botanyconference.org/engine/search/index.php?func=detail&aid=1127 An overview of the genus ''Setaria'' (Poaceae: Panicoideae: Paniceae) in the Old World: Systematic revision and phylogenetic approach.] Abstract. Botany 2004. Salt Lake City. August 3, 2004.</ref> and members are commonly known as '''foxtail''' or '''bristle grasses'''.<ref name="GRIN"/><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=130214 Flora of China Vol. 22 Page 1, 499, 531 <big>狗尾草属</big> gou wei cao shu ''Setaria'' P. Beauvois, Ess. Agrostogr. 51. 1812]</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/NAPA/TaxonMaps/Genus/County/Setaria Biota of North America Program 2013 county distribution maps]</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/floraspecie.php?genere=setaria Altervista Flora Italiana] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150201022105/http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/floraspecie.php?genere=Setaria |date=2015-02-01 }}</ref><ref>[http://bie.ala.org.au/species/SETARIA Atlas of Living Australia]</ref><ref>[http://redlist.sanbi.org/genus.php?genus=1167 Sanbi Red List of South African Plants]</ref>

==Description==
The grass is topped by a cylindrical long-haired head, which tend to droop when ripe. The seeds are less than {{Convert|6|mm|abbr=off|frac=8}} in length.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |others=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |pages=56 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref>

Numerous species were once considered members of ''Setaria'' but have since been reassigned to the genera ''[[Brachiaria]]'', ''[[Dissochondrus]]'', ''[[Echinochloa]]'', ''[[Holcolemma]]'', ''[[Ixophorus]]'', ''[[Oplismenus]]'', ''[[Panicum]]'', ''[[Pennisetum]]'', ''[[Pseudoraphis]]'', ''[[Setariopsis]]'', and ''[[Urochloa]]''.

== Uses ==
The grains can be eaten raw, though are hard and can be bitter; boiling can reduce both of these properties.<ref name=":0" />

Several species have been domesticated and used as staple crops throughout history: [[foxtail millet]] (''S. italica''), korali (''[[Setaria pumila|S. pumila]]'') in India, and, before the full domestication of [[maize]], ''[[Setaria macrostachya]]'' in Mexico.<ref name="DiaoJia2017">{{cite book |last1=Diao |first1=Xianmin |title=Genetics and Genomics of Setaria |last2=Jia |first2=Guanqing |year=2017 |isbn=978-3-319-45103-9 |series=Plant Genetics and Genomics: Crops and Models |volume=19 |pages=61–72 |chapter=Origin and Domestication of Foxtail Millet |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-45105-3_4 |issn=2363-9601}}</ref> Several species are still cultivated today as food or as animal fodder, such as foxtail millet and korali (''[[Setaria pumila|S. pumila]]''), while others are considered [[Invasive species|invasive weeds]].<ref name="Dekker">{{cite book |last=Dekker |first=Jack |title=Weed Biology and Management |date=29 February 2004 |publisher=Kluwer Academic Publishers |isbn=9781402017612 |editor=Inderjit |pages=65–67 |chapter=4}}</ref> ''S. italica'' and ''[[Setaria viridis|S. viridis]]'' are being developed as genetic model systems for the study of [[Monocotyledon|monocots]] and [[bioenergy]] grasses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Li |first1=P. |last2=Brutnell |first2=T. P. |date=2011-03-31 |title=Setaria viridis and Setaria italica, model genetic systems for the Panicoid grasses |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/jxb/err096 |journal=Journal of Experimental Botany |volume=62 |issue=9 |pages=3031–3037 |doi=10.1093/jxb/err096 |pmid=21459768 |issn=0022-0957}}</ref>

Other species that have been cultivated as crops include ''[[Setaria palmifolia|S. palmifolia]]'' (highland pitpit) of [[Papua New Guinea]], where it is cultivated as a green vegetable; ''[[Setaria parviflora|S. parviflora]]'' (knot-root foxtail), historically cultivated in [[Mesoamerica]]; and ''[[Setaria sphacelata|S. sphacelata]]'' (African bristle grass) of Sudan, a "lost millet" of [[Nubia]].<ref name="Fuller 2014">{{cite book |last=Fuller |first=Dorian Q. |title=Encyclopedia of Global Archaeology |publisher=Springer New York |year=2014 |publication-place=New York, NY |pages=4945–4948 |chapter=Millets: Origins and Development |doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-0465-2_2181|isbn=978-1-4419-0426-3 |s2cid=129203615 }}</ref>
